title: Prayer Garden Waiver
subject: Contracts
stem:
BARMATRIX Q# 14460 — Christian variation: 14460_prayer_garden_waiver

Martha, a property owner, and Barnabas, a landscape architect, signed a detailed writing in which Barnabas agreed to landscape Martha's residential property — including a quiet prayer garden — in accordance with a design Barnabas prepared and incorporated in the writing. Martha agreed to pay $10,000 for the work upon its completion. Martha's husband, Timothy, was not a party to the agreement and had no ownership interest in the premises. At Martha's insistence, the written agreement contained a provision that neither party would be bound unless Ruth, Martha's law partner and an avid student of landscaping, should approve Barnabas's design. Before Barnabas commenced the work, Ruth, in the presence of both Martha and Barnabas, expressly disapproved the landscaping design. Nevertheless, Martha ordered Barnabas to proceed with the work, and Barnabas reluctantly did so. When Barnabas's performance was 40% complete, Martha repudiated her duty, if any, to pay the contract price or any part thereof.

If Barnabas now sues Martha for damages for breach of contract, which of the following concepts best supports Barnabas's claim?
call: If Barnabas now sues Martha for damages for breach of contract, which of the following concepts best supports Barnabas's claim?
rightExplanation:
C is correct. Gold Key: A party may waive an express condition that exists for her own benefit, even after the condition has failed; once the other side materially relies on the waiver — here, by performing 40% of the work — the waiver cannot be retracted. The approval condition was inserted at Martha's insistence and protected her. When Ruth expressly disapproved, the condition failed; when Martha then ordered Barnabas to proceed, she waived it. Barnabas's 40% performance is the reliance that locks the waiver in, so Martha's duty to pay is enforceable and her repudiation is a breach.

Silver Key: The call asks which concept supports damages for breach of contract. Cut every choice naming an off-contract backup theory — the winning concept must live inside the contract and explain why the failed condition no longer matters. Only C does both.

wrongExplanations.A: This choice reaches for the most familiar performance doctrine, and Barnabas did perform real work under a real design. It misses that the stem caps performance at 40% complete — "substantial performance" overclaims against that number on its face. Gold Key: substantial performance softens only constructive conditions; the approval term here is an express condition, which demands strict compliance unless waived or excused — so the doctrine never even reaches this stem.
wrongExplanations.B: This choice hears "ordered Barnabas to proceed and he reluctantly did so" as reliance on a promise, which is the promissory-estoppel fact pattern. It misses that a signed, bargained-for contract already exists — estoppel is the substitute theory for when there is no enforceable contract, and Barnabas can sue on the actual contract. Gold Key: promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment are no-contract backup theories; when a valid contract covers the dispute, sue on the contract.
wrongExplanations.D: This choice sees Martha keeping 40% of a landscaping job without paying and reaches for the fairness theory that fits that picture. It misses that the call asks which concept supports a claim for damages for breach of contract — unjust enrichment is the off-contract restitution backup, not a breach concept. Silver Key: when the call locks "breach of contract," cut the off-contract backup theories first; the fairness pull of D is exactly the engineered trap.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text:
- A is cut on a visible overclaim: the answer's own word "substantial" collides with the stem's stated "40% complete." A student needs no doctrine to see that 40% is not substantially everything. (The deeper express-vs-constructive point stays in lawyer confirmation.)
- B and D are cut at the call with the backup-theories anchor: the call demands a concept supporting damages for breach of contract; promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment are taught as the no-contract backup theories, and the stem hands the student a signed, detailed, bargained-for contract.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: If A is kept alive, the surviving pair A vs. C clashes on one axis: which doctrine answers the actual obstacle in this stem — incomplete performance, or a failed express condition? The splitting fact is Ruth's express disapproval followed by Martha's order to proceed: the obstacle is the condition, and only C speaks to it.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: The Gold Key locks it: a benefited party may waive an express condition even after it fails, and reliance by part performance makes the waiver irrevocable. Residual answer: C.

studentScript: The call says breach of contract. B and D are no-contract backup theories — cut. A says substantial, but the stem says 40% — cut. The real obstacle is the disapproved design, and Martha ordered the work forward anyway: she waived the condition, and Barnabas's 40% reliance makes it stick. Pick C.

A.signal: The choice's own word 'substantial' collides with the stem's stated '40% complete' — a visible answer-text-vs-stem-fact mismatch.
A.lawyer: Substantial performance satisfies only constructive conditions of exchange despite immaterial deviations (Jacob & Youngs v. Kent; Restatement (Second) § 237 cmt. d); it does not excuse non-occurrence of an express condition, and 40% would not be substantial regardless.

B.signal: The stem hands the student a signed, detailed, bargained contract; with the backup-theories anchor, a substitute-for-contract theory cannot be the BEST concept.
B.lawyer: Promissory estoppel (Restatement (Second) § 90) substitutes for consideration where no enforceable bargain exists; consideration is undisputed here, so suing on the actual contract is the direct and stronger theory.

C.signal: Only this concept speaks to the stem's actual obstacle — the disapproved design condition — and explains why the duty to pay still binds.
C.lawyer: Martha waived the approval condition for her benefit by ordering performance after its non-occurrence; under Restatement (Second) § 84(2) the waiver became irrevocable when Barnabas materially relied by performing to 40%.

D.signal: The call locks 'damages for breach of contract'; with the backup-theories anchor, a restitution theory answers a different claim than the one the call names.
D.lawyer: Unjust enrichment is off-contract restitution; a valid enforceable contract displaces it as to matters the contract governs (Restatement (Third) of Restitution § 2(2)), and it does not support breach-of-contract damages.

goldKeys.unlocks: C is the concept that keeps the contract claim alive despite the failed approval condition.

remediation.title: Failed condition? Look for the waiver
remediation.signal: An express condition fails, but the protected party pushes the deal forward anyway and later refuses to pay.
remediation.studentMove: Cut off-contract backup theories at the call, check quantity words against stem numbers, then ask which concept clears the failed condition.
remediation.tinyRule: Ordering performance after a condition fails waives the condition; part performance in reliance makes the waiver irrevocable.
remediation.trap: Picking unjust enrichment because keeping 40% of a job unpaid feels like the unfairness being tested.
